extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory mathematical logic, set theory, and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for correctly using logical notation, understanding free vs. bound variables, forming truth sets, and performing operations on sets (union, intersection, difference), including how to reason about these via logical equivalences, Venn diagrams, and truth tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish free and bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Free variables stand for objects that the statement says something about and plugging different values for a free variable may change the truth value; bound variables are letters used as a convenience that should not be thought to stand for any particular object and can be replaced without changing meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show that x can be free in one statement (e.g., x^2 < 9) but bound when used in set-builder notation ({x | x^2 < 9}). Bound variables may be eliminated by rephrasing; always identify which variables are free vs. bound when analyzing statements. Anti-pattern: treating a bound variable as if it denotes a particular object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret set-builder / elementhood notation correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression {x | P(x)} is a name for a set (not a statement); the statement y ∈ {x | P(x)} means the same thing as P(y), and y ∉ {x | P(x)} means ¬P(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading expressions involving elementhood tests, translate elementhood into the corresponding predicate about the element. Example: y ∈ {x | x^2 < 9} ↔ y^2 < 9. Do not confuse a set-expression with a logical statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and use truth sets
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth set of a statement P(x) (with one free variable) is the set of all values of x that make P(x) true, i.e., Truth set of P(x) = {x | P(x)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth sets to distinguish values that make predicates true vs false. Note this definition as stated applies to statements with one free variable (extensions for multiple free variables are treated later). Examples: {n | n is an even prime} = {2}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify the universe of discourse / range of variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables range over a universe U (set of all possible values). Although often implicit from context, the universe can be explicitly indicated, e.g., {x ∈ U | P(x)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common universes are named R, Q, Z, N; superscripts +/− indicate positive/negative subsets. The choice of universe affects truth sets (e.g., {x ∈ R | x^2 < 9} vs {x ∈ Z | x^2 < 9}). Use explicit universe notation to avoid ambiguity or to temporarily restrict attention (e.g., {x ∈ R+ | x^2 < 9}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explicit restriction notation for subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: The notation {x ∈ A | P(x)} indicates elements must both belong to A and satisfy P(x); equivalently, y ∈ {x ∈ A | P(x)} ↔ (y ∈ A ∧ P(y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notation can be used to restrict the universe or to focus on a part of it. View membership as requiring passing multiple tests (e.g., be in A and satisfy P).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize extreme truth sets (universal and empty)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P(x) is true for every x ∈ U then its truth set is U; if P(x) is false for every x ∈ U then its truth set is the empty set ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate to tautologies and contradictions: e.g., P(x) ∨ ¬P(x) (a tautology) has truth set U. Example: x^2 ≥ 0 has truth set R. Use this to reason about existence/nonexistence of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand empty set notation and distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The empty set ∅ = { } is the unique set with no elements; {∅} is not the same as ∅ (it is a set whose single element is ∅).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse elements with singleton sets (e.g., 2 ≠ {2}; 2 ∈ {2} but 2 ≠ {2}). Use correct notation when reasoning about emptiness and singletons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of basic set operations (intersection, union, difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}; A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B} (inclusive or); A \ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate set operations into corresponding elementhood logical forms when analyzing membership. Examples provided with finite sets and predicate-based sets (e.g., men with brown hair).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate set operations to logical connectives but do not conflate them
rubrics_metrics.description: Set-theory operations correspond to logical connectives (∩ ↔ ∧, ∪ ↔ ∨, \ ↔ ∧¬), but logical connectives combine statements while set operations combine sets and so expressions like A ∧ B or P(x) ∩ Q(x) are meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When A and B are truth sets of predicates P(x) and Q(x), A ∩ B is the truth set of P(x) ∧ Q(x), etc. Always ensure you apply connectives to statements and set operations to sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Venn diagrams to visualize set operations and identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent the universe as a rectangle and sets as circles; shaded regions correspond to set-results (e.g., A ∩ B, A ∪ B, A \ B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venn diagrams help verify identities and show disjointness or subset relations. Note limitation: overlapping circles easily depict up to three sets; four-set Venn diagrams are not possible with overlapping circles and require other shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric difference identity and visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: The symmetric difference A Δ B equals (A \ B) ∪ (B \ A) and also equals (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can confirm this equality by Venn diagrams or by translating to logical forms for element membership. Use this identity when reasoning about elements in exactly one of the sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate combined logical statements to corresponding truth sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is truth set of P(x) and B of Q(x), then truth set of P(x) ∧ Q(x) is A ∩ B, of P(x) ∨ Q(x) is A ∪ B, and of ¬P(x) is U \ A (where U is universe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these correspondences to reason about truth sets of compound predicates and to compute sets by logical combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive set identities by rewriting membership with logical equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove set equalities or other identities, write x ∈ (set-expression) as a logical formula using ∧, ∨, ¬, then apply logical equivalences (DeMorgan, distributive laws, etc.) or use truth tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show derivation of distributive laws (A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)), DeMorgan-style identities for difference, and other identities. Method: expand definitions → simplify logically → convert back to set notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and recognition of subset and disjointness
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊆ B iff every element of A is an element of B. A and B are disjoint if A ∩ B = ∅ (no elements in common).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Venn diagrams to reflect these relations and deduce consequences (e.g., A ∩ B and A \ B are always disjoint). Verify with elementwise logical forms when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use deductive logical reasoning in set proofs; avoid imprecise intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove set-theoretic claims by showing membership implications using the logical forms of membership statements and known logical rules; do not rely solely on intuitive 'start/add/remove' narratives which can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example proof: For any sets A and B, (A ∪ B) \ B ⊆ A is proven by showing x ∈ (A ∪ B) \ B implies x ∈ A using the logical form (x ∈ A ∨ x ∈ B) ∧ ¬(x ∈ B) and deducing x ∈ A (instance of P ∨ Q and ¬Q ⇒ P). Exercises challenge intuitive but incorrect conclusions like (A ∪ B) \ B = A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze and simplify elementhood statements systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: When given complex membership statements (e.g., x ∈ A ∩ (B ∪ C)), rewrite stepwise using definitions to obtain equivalent logical formulas (x ∈ A ∧ (x ∈ B ∨ x ∈ C)), then simplify using logical equivalences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow worked examples to practice converting membership into logical structure, recognizing equivalent forms, and using laws (e.g., distributive) to show set equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use truth tables to verify logical equivalences that underlie set identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some set equalities correspond to propositional equivalences; verify these by constructing a truth table for the propositional formulas (e.g., show (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬(P ∧ Q) is equivalent to (P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ (Q ∧ ¬P)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute P ≡ (x ∈ A), Q ≡ (x ∈ B) to convert propositional results into set-theoretic conclusions. This is an alternative to algebraic logical equivalences or Venn diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and form conditional (→) as logical connective and its truth-table
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditional P → Q is true in all cases except when P is true and Q is false; P → Q is logically equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples with predicates P(x) and Q(x) to determine truth-table rows and to justify equivalence with ¬P ∨ Q. Understand ordinary-language mappings (threatening teacher example) where ¬P ∨ Q and P → Q convey the same intent.
